content: 1. Exclusion of Patients Lost to Follow-Up: The data excludes individuals who were lost to follow-up during tuberculosis (TB) treatment. This information is sourced from the WHO expert consultation meeting report on drug-resistant TB treatment outcome definitions, held from November 17–19, 2020. 2. Recommended Investigations for TB Treatment Follow-Up: Clinical Evaluation (including nutritional assessment): Conducted monthly during treatment and at months 3, 6, and 12 after treatment completion. Sputum Smear Microscopy: Performed at months 2, 5, and at the end of treatment. For drug-resistant TB, it is done monthly and at months 3, 6, and 12 post-treatment. Bacteriological Culture: Recommended when there is no response to treatment, at month 6, and monthly for drug-resistant TB. Post-treatment, it is done at months 3, 6, and 12. Drug Susceptibility Testing: Conducted when culture results are positive. Chest Radiography: Performed at months 6, 12, and at the end of treatment. Serum Glucose: Checked in the first month of treatment. HIV Counseling and Testing: Conducted in the first month and repeated if necessary. Mental Health Assessment: Performed in the first month of treatment. Liver Function Tests: Conducted in the first month and monthly if the patient is on bedaquiline (Bdq). Kidney Function and Electrolytes: Assessed in the first month. Thyroid Function: Checked in the first month and every three months if the patient is on ethionamide (Eto) or prothionamide (Pto). Hemoglobin and Blood Count: Monitored in the first month and every three months if the patient is on linezolid (Lzd). Vision Function: Assessed in the first month and repeated if necessary for patients on ethambutol (E) or linezolid (Lzd). Audiometry: Conducted monthly for patients on injectable drugs. Electrocardiogram (ECG): Performed at months 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and at the end of treatment for patients on bedaquiline (Bdq), moxifloxacin (Mfx), clofazimine (Cfz), or delamanid (Dlm). 3. Management of TB Treatment Interruptions: If treatment is interrupted for less than 2 weeks, the previous treatment regimen is continued from the point it was stopped. For interruptions lasting 2–7 weeks: If the sputum smear is negative, the previous treatment is restarted. If the sputum smear is positive, a new treatment regimen is initiated based on drug susceptibility test results. For interruptions of 8 weeks or more: If the sputum smear is negative, the previous treatment is restarted. If the sputum smear is positive, a new treatment regimen is initiated based on drug susceptibility test results. 4. Role of Community Health Workers in TB Management: Early Identification of TB Patients: Actively identify individuals with TB symptoms in the community and refer them to health centers. Trace and refer close contacts of confirmed TB patients, especially those with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or living with HIV. Treatment Support: Supervise and support patients in taking TB medications, provide reminders about adverse drug effects, and encourage adherence to treatment. Patient and Family Support: Address psychological barriers to treatment, coordinate with health staff for social and psychological support, and provide motivational messages to patients. Monitoring Treatment Progress: Remind patients about follow-up visits and assist them in attending health facility appointments. Social Mobilization: Educate the community about TB, address stigma, and promote early diagnosis and treatment. Tracing Patients Lost to Follow-Up: Locate patients who miss treatment, determine reasons for non-adherence, and facilitate re-initiation of treatment. 5. Collection, Storage, and Transport of Biological Specimens for TB: Specimen Collection: Sputum specimens should be collected outdoors or in well-ventilated rooms to minimize exposure to infectious aerosols. Patients should be instructed to produce sputum from the lower airways through deep coughing. Specimens must be collected in sterile, leak-proof containers and labeled accurately. Specimen Storage: Sputum specimens should be refrigerated at 2–8°C if not processed on the same day. Urine specimens should be processed within 8 hours if kept at room temperature or refrigerated/frozen depending on the delay. Specimen Transport: Specimens should ideally be delivered to the laboratory on the same day of collection. For longer distances, specimens must be transported within 48 hours, kept refrigerated, and packed using triple packaging to ensure biosafety. 6. WHO-Recommended TB Treatment Regimens Based on Drug Resistance: Drug-Susceptible TB: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (2HRZE), followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin (4HR). Isoniazid-Resistant TB: 6 months of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin (6(H)REZ-Lfx). Rifampicin-Resistant or Multidrug-Resistant TB (RR/MDR-TB): Shorter all-oral regimen: 4–6 months of bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, and ethionamide, followed by 5 months of levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Longer regimen: 18 months of bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, linezolid, clofazimine, and cycloserine, tailored to the patient’s eligibility.
